issues.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence does not, by itself, require the prosecution case to be disbelieved.
material_facts: The accused sustained injuries during the same incident in which the deceased was attacked.
The prosecution did not explain those injuries apart from a statement in the complaint.
The eyewitness accounts were corroborated by medical evidence.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s unexplained injuries made it important to investigate the genesis of the occurrence, but they did not by themselves require rejection of the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing (2001) 6 SCC 145, relying on Rajender Singh v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 298, Ram Sunder Yadav v. State of Bihar (1998) 7 SCC 365, and Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190, the prosecution is not invariably obliged to explain injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence. Before non-explanation may affect the prosecution case, the injuries must have been serious and sustained during the occurrence. Even then, clear, cogent and credible evidence may prevent non-explanation from being a basis to reject the prosecution case.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal from a conviction for causing a death.
predicates.accused_injuries_in_same_occurrence: The accused sustained injuries in the occurrence in which the deceased was injured.
predicates.accused_injuries_serious: The accused’s injuries were serious in nature.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_cogent_and_cr: The prosecution evidence was clear, cogent and credible.

issues.definition: When a death-conviction appeal involves accused injuries from the same occurrence, serious injuries or clear, cogent and credible prosecution evidence means that the failure to explain those injuries does not alone discredit the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: A homicide committed without premeditation during a sudden fight in the heat of passion falls within the sudden-fight exception when the offender takes no undue advantage and acts neither cruelly nor unusually.
material_facts: The parties had assembled to discuss a dispute, and there was an exchange of words followed by a scuffle in which both sides sustained injuries.
There was no clear evidence of who started the attack, and the parties had initially been unarmed.
During the scuffle, one accused went inside a nearby room, brought an axe and struck the deceased on the head.
The deceased survived for about a month, and the Court found that the accused had not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
issues.conclusion: The acts fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies where the act is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner. All its ingredients must be established. Sridhar Bhuyan v. State of Orissa (2004) 11 SCC 395 explains that the fight involves mutual provocation and blows and that whether a quarrel was sudden depends on the proved facts.

rule.if: homicide_conviction_appeal and no_premeditation and sudden_fight_in_heat_of_passion and fight_with_deceased and not undue_advantage_taken and not cruel_or_unusual_conduct

predicates.no_premeditation: The act was not planned or deliberated beforehand.
predicates.sudden_fight_in_heat_of_passion: A sudden quarrel led to a fight while the participants were in the heat of passion.
predicates.fight_with_deceased: The fight was with the person who died.

issues.definition: In an appeal involving a death, the sudden-fight exception applies when an unpremeditated fight in the heat of passion is with the deceased and the offender neither takes an unfair advantage nor acts cruelly or unusually.

issues.legal_issue: When the sudden-fight exception applies but the offender intended to inflict an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offence is culpable homicide rather than murder, with the higher degree of culpable homicide applying.
material_facts: The deceased was struck on the head with an axe and sustained multiple fractures and brain injuries.
The Court found that the weapon and manner of the blow established an intention to inflict the injury that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The Court found that the act fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
issues.conclusion: The murder conviction was modified to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC.
issues.legal_principle: The third clause of Section 300 IPC requires proof both that the offender intended to inflict the injury and that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Nankaunoo v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2016) 3 SCC 317 explains that sufficiency means a high probability of death in the ordinary course of nature and is assessed with regard to such matters as the weapon and the part of the body injured. Where the sudden-fight exception applies, but the offender intended to inflict an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the conviction is for culpable homicide under Section 304 Part I IPC.
